arguments.title: Recurring flat tire: what to check and what to tell the workshop
arguments.excerpt: A flat tire that keeps coming back usually leaves clues. Here is what to look at before you visit, and the details our workshop asks for when you drop the bike off.
arguments.summary: Practical search-led guide helping bike owners describe a repeating flat tire before a workshop visit. Complements the puncture repair service page (post 100).
arguments.reasoning: Workflow-planned niche topic anchored to the puncture repair service page. Distinct reader task: preparing observations for a repair visit, not describing the service itself. Author set to the existing Workshop Team account.
arguments.content:
A puncture that happens once is bad luck. A tire that goes soft again a few days after it was fixed usually means something on the bike is still causing it. The good news is that the pattern of the air loss tells you a lot, and it costs nothing to write it down before you bring the bike in.

Note how fast the air goes

Pump the tire up to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall, then check it again at set intervals. Three rough patterns are worth reporting:

  • Flat within minutes. A large hole, a torn tube, or a valve that is not sealing.
  • Soft after a few hours or overnight. A small puncture, a slow valve leak, or in some tube types normal seepage that is faster than you expect.
  • Only flat after riding. Often linked to something that moves or presses under load, such as a spoke end, damaged rim tape, or a low pressure pinch.

Write down the times. "Down from 4 bar to nothing in about six hours" is far more useful to a mechanic than "it keeps going flat".

Check the outside of the tire

With the wheel still on the bike, turn it slowly and look over the whole tread. Run a gloved hand or a rag lightly along the surface so you do not cut a finger on whatever is stuck in there. Look for:

  • Glass, grit, wire or thorns pressed into the rubber
  • Cuts that go deep enough to show the fabric underneath
  • Bulges or a section of tread that sits unevenly in the rim
  • Sidewall cracking, which is common on bikes that stood unused for a long time

If you find something sharp, leave it in place and tell us where it is. Its position helps line up the hole in the tube with the hole in the tire.

Check the valve

Put a drop of water or spit on the open valve with the tire inflated. A bubble that keeps growing points at the valve rather than the tube body. Also check that the valve sits straight through the rim hole. A valve pulled to one side gets stressed every ride and can tear where it meets the tube.

Think about where the flats keep happening

Two more things worth noting:

  • Same wheel every time? A problem that always returns on the rear wheel suggests the wheel, rim tape or load, not the road.
  • Same route every time? A stretch of road with hedge cuttings or broken glass can explain repeat punctures on an otherwise healthy wheel.

Pressure and load

Repeat flats are often a pressure story. A tire run well below its marked range squashes the tube against the rim edge on kerbs and potholes. Note the pressure you normally ride at, whether you check it with a gauge or by squeezing the tire, and whether the bike carries panniers, a child seat or heavy loads. It changes what pressure is sensible for you.

What to bring to the workshop

Bring the bike itself, and if you have them, the old tubes from previous repairs. A used tube shows where the hole was, and a hole on the rim side rather than the tread side points at the rim tape instead of the road. Bring your written notes too, covering:

  • When the tire was last inflated and how quickly it went down
  • Which wheel is affected
  • How many times it has been repaired recently
  • Anything you already found in the tread
  • Your usual riding surface and load

When to stop riding on it

Riding on a tire that is almost empty risks damage to the rim and to the tire casing, which turns a cheap fix into a larger one. If the tire will not hold air long enough for the trip, it is better to walk the bike or arrange transport to the workshop.

How we take it from there

Our workshop repairs bicycle tire punctures and inspects tires. When you bring the bike in, describe when the air loss happens and we work through the tube, the tire and the rim to find the cause behind the repeat flats. You can read more on our bicycle puncture repair page.
